notes: Frame this as an allocation problem, not a technology debate. Point to Banaskantha and Rajkot as the clearest mismatch between water-stressed production and still-partial adoption. Expect a question on whether the state already scaled enough; answer that the lag in key districts is exactly where incremental income resilience remains available.
title: Micro-irrigation expansion improved resilience in Gujarat, but adoption still trails in districts where water-productivity gains matter most
subtitle: Statewide scaling proved the model, yet the remaining income opportunity sits in specific high-output districts where irrigation dependence is high and efficient water use is still not the dominant production practice.

chart.annotation: Water-stressed farm belts still show only partial micro-irrigation coverage, leaving resilience and water-productivity gains uncaptured.
chart.source: Source: DES Gujarat agri stats; state micro-irrigation program reporting 2024-2025 [[src:official]]

insights.text: **Banaskantha** shows the clearest gap: **64** net irrigated area share versus **31** micro-irrigation area share, meaning one of Gujarat’s most water-dependent production belts still has large room to raise water productivity through targeted adoption.

The same pattern runs across **Rajkot** (**47** vs **28**), **Junagadh** (**52** vs **34**), and **Surendranagar** (**44** vs **26**), showing expansion has been meaningful but not sufficient in major commercial districts.

Even lower-gap districts such as **Ahmedabad** (**41** vs **22**) and **Kheda** (**39** vs **19**) remain far from full coverage, which supports a district-specific push rather than treating statewide rollout as complete.

footnote: Net irrigated area share and micro-irrigation area share are shown together to evidence where efficient water-use adoption still lags water dependence. Source: DES Gujarat; state micro-irrigation program reporting 2024-2025 [[src:official]]
